session.question: How cross-disciplinary collaborations help sustainability education for manufacturing teams facing digitalization and skill changes?
session.answer:
Cross-disciplinary collaboration helps sustainability education by combining digital, green, and manufacturing perspectives to anticipate how skill requirements are changing in European manufacturing. In practice, this allows organizations to identify both current and future transversal skills needed for industrial symbiosis and energy efficiency, rather than training only for existing roles. An automated skill database can then support companies, education and training institutions, and policymakers in designing targeted training programmes and strategy roadmaps for a digitally enabled and sustainable manufacturing sector. (akyazi2022identifyingfutureskill chunk 1)

More broadly, interdisciplinary collaboration supports knowledge integration by pairing epistemic stability, which enables participants to contribute their own domain expertise with methodological confidence, with epistemic adaptability, which enables openness to others’ knowledge, curiosity, and effective communication. For manufacturing teams, this means integrating technical, environmental, and organizational knowledge to respond to digitalization and workforce change. (horn2022epistemicstabilityand chunk 1)

Cross-disciplinary work also helps teams understand adoption challenges more holistically, including job displacement, trust, privacy, and human factors associated with digital manufacturing and human-robot collaboration. By bringing together employees, legal experts, consultants, and ethicists, organizations can develop responsible implementation roadmaps that better align technology adoption with workforce sustainability. (leesakul2022workplace4.0exploring chunk 1)

Finally, interdisciplinary learning can improve understanding of power relations, decision-making, and value conflicts that shape sustainability transitions, thereby supporting more robust and long-term educational and organizational responses. (feeney2022organizationslearningand chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-c4424935: The paper argues that European manufacturing is being reshaped by digitalisation and sustainability demands, so companies need a multi-skilled workforce and updated training strategies. To support this, the authors built an automated manufacturing skill database that includes both current and future skill needs for transversal occupations related to industrial symbiosis and energy efficiency. The database is intended as a tool for companies, education and training institutions, and policymakers to develop training programmes and strategy roadmaps. This suggests cross-disciplinary collaboration helps sustainability education by combining insights from digital, green, and manufacturing domains to anticipate changing skill requirements and align workforce development with future industrial changes.
From Tugce Akyazi, Patricia del Val, Aitor Goti, and Aitor Oyarbide-Zubillaga. Identifying future skill requirements of the job profiles for a sustainable european manufacturing industry 4.0. Recycling, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/recycling7030032, doi:10.3390/recycling7030032.

pqac-6b38f981: The excerpt describes how digitalisation and sustainability needs are reshaping European manufacturing and argues that companies need a multi-skilled workforce to manage both technological developments and green transformation. To support this, the authors developed an automated skill database for transversal manufacturing occupations related to industrial symbiosis and energy efficiency, including both current and future skill needs. The paper suggests that such a resource can help companies, education and training institutions, and policymakers design training programmes and strategy roadmaps that anticipate new skill requirements caused by industrial and sustainability changes. This implies that cross-functional collaboration helps identify emerging skills and align workforce development with digital and green transitions.
From Tugce Akyazi, Patricia del Val, Aitor Goti, and Aitor Oyarbide-Zubillaga. Identifying future skill requirements of the job profiles for a sustainable european manufacturing industry 4.0. Recycling, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/recycling7030032, doi:10.3390/recycling7030032.

pqac-ec4fb97b: The excerpt explains that global sustainability challenges require interdisciplinary approaches and cross-disciplinary collaboration. It proposes two competency sets needed for interdisciplinary knowledge integration: Epistemic Stability (ES), which helps people contribute their own expertise through theoretical/methodological grounding and confidence, and Epistemic Adaptability (EA), which helps people engage with others’ knowledge through curiosity, openness, and communication. The paper argues that these competencies support assessment, management, and training for future professionals working on sustainability issues. For manufacturing teams facing digitalization and changing skill requirements, cross-disciplinary collaboration would similarly help integrate diverse knowledge and adapt to new demands.
From Annemarie Horn, Eduardo Urias, and Marjolein Zweekhorst. Epistemic stability and epistemic adaptability: interdisciplinary knowledge integration competencies for complex sustainability issues. Sustainability Science, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11625-022-01113-2, doi:10.1007/s11625-022-01113-2.

pqac-81631a3e: The excerpt argues that sustainability challenges are better addressed when organizations broaden their thinking, go beyond organizational boundaries, and collaborate with diverse stakeholders. Learning is presented as a key process for handling the political and process-related tensions that arise in such collaborative action. A cross-disciplinary review shows that perspectives from business, management, environmental science, sociology, policy, urban planning, and development help reveal common themes and challenges. Interdisciplinary work can improve understanding of power relations, decision-making, and entrenched value structures that limit meaningful sustainability solutions. The paper suggests that prioritizing sustainability outcomes over firm performance and breaking ‘reflexive complicity’ can support more radical, long-term responses.
From Melanie Feeney, Therese Grohnert, Wim Gijselaers, and Pim Martens. Organizations, learning, and sustainability: a cross-disciplinary review and research agenda. Journal of Business Ethics, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-022-05072-7, doi:10.1007/s10551-022-05072-7.

pqac-be948ab4: The excerpt discusses how digital manufacturing technologies and human-robot collaboration raise workforce concerns such as job displacement, acceptance, trust, and privacy. The paper argues that understanding wider human factors is crucial for strategically adopting technology and recommends interventions at both individual and organisational levels. It also notes the importance of gathering perspectives from multiple stakeholders, including employees, legal experts, consultants, and ethicists, to build a roadmap for responsible implementation and a sustainable workforce. This implies that interdisciplinary or cross-functional collaboration helps address adoption challenges more holistically and supports responsible digital transformation.
From Natalie Leesakul, Anne‐Marie Oostveen, Iveta Eimontaite, Max L. Wilson, and Richard Hyde. Workplace 4.0: exploring the implications of technology adoption in digital manufacturing on a sustainable workforce. Sustainability, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/su14063311, doi:10.3390/su14063311.

The paper suggests that such a resource can help companies, education and training institutions, and policymakers design training programmes and strategy roadmaps that anticipate new skill requirements caused by industrial and sustainability changes. This implies that cross-functional collaboration helps identify emerging skills and align workforce development with digital and green transitions.
contexts.question: What benefits do interdisciplinary or cross-functional collaborations bring to sustainability learning, green skills, and digital transformation in manufacturing?

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How cross-disciplinary collaborations help sustainability education for manufacturing teams facing digitalization and skill changes?

Cross-disciplinary collaboration helps sustainability education by combining digital, green, and manufacturing perspectives to anticipate how skill requirements are changing in European manufacturing. In practice, this allows organizations to identify both current and future transversal skills needed for industrial symbiosis and energy efficiency, rather than training only for existing roles. An automated skill database can then support companies, education and training institutions, and policymakers in designing targeted training programmes and strategy roadmaps for a digitally enabled and sustainable manufacturing sector. (akyazi2022identifyingfutureskill chunk 1)

More broadly, interdisciplinary collaboration supports knowledge integration by pairing epistemic stability, which enables participants to contribute their own domain expertise with methodological confidence, with epistemic adaptability, which enables openness to others’ knowledge, curiosity, and effective communication. For manufacturing teams, this means integrating technical, environmental, and organizational knowledge to respond to digitalization and workforce change. (horn2022epistemicstabilityand chunk 1)

Cross-disciplinary work also helps teams understand adoption challenges more holistically, including job displacement, trust, privacy, and human factors associated with digital manufacturing and human-robot collaboration. By bringing together employees, legal experts, consultants, and ethicists, organizations can develop responsible implementation roadmaps that better align technology adoption with workforce sustainability. (leesakul2022workplace4.0exploring chunk 1)

Finally, interdisciplinary learning can improve understanding of power relations, decision-making, and value conflicts that shape sustainability transitions, thereby supporting more robust and long-term educational and organizational responses. (feeney2022organizationslearningand chunk 1)
